newsitem.title: BULGARIA: Bulgaria's opposition UDF launch election campaign.
newsitem.headline: Bulgaria's opposition UDF launch election campaign.

text.p: Some 5,000 supporters of Bulgaria's Union of Democratic Forces (UDF), favourites to win general elections on April 19, gathered in central Sofia on Sunday to launch their election campaign.
The UDF led 30 days of mass protests which forced the ruling ex-communist Socialist Party to stand down last month. Elections have been called 20 months ahead of schedule.

The UDF and its coalition allies are expected to win a majority in the new parliament, the Socialists losing support because of a deep economic crisis. Their candidate suffered defeat in 1996 presidential elections won by Petar Stoyanov, who ran on the UDF ticket.
"Now the road goes through a strong parliamentary majority, which...must take responsibility for ruling the country," said UDF leader Ivan Kostov.
The interim cabinet, led by Sofia's UDF mayor Stefan Sofianski, has taken first steps towards containing economic chaos and averting collapse.
The cabinet has committed itself to strict financial discipline to prepare for implementation of a fixed exchange rate regime by the new government in June.

On Monday, the International Monetary Fund and the interim government announced a new standby accord and an emergency payment to buy grain totalling more than $650 million, giving Bulgaria a prospect of relief from its heavy debt burden and four-digit annual inflation.

The World Bank said on Friday it was considering $290 million in loans to support economic reform efforts in Bulgaria following discussions in Washington with a delegation from the Bulgarian government, headed by Sofianski.
"The priorities of the Union of Democratic Forces will be stabilisation of the economy, privatisation and attracting foreign investors," Kostov said.
Bulgaria suffers the lowest foreign investment in eastern Europe, amounting to $1 billion since 1989.
All Bulgaria's political parties have pledged their support for the tough reform programme and both Stoyanov and Sofianski have warned that the measures will be painful.
"Wide support and a stable parliamentary majority are needed for the implementation of the necessary changes and a strict financial regime," Kostov told the rally.
The UDF, which used to be an alliance of 17 groups, became a single political party last month in a bid to adjust to the task of governing the Balkan country.
The UDF formed the first non-communist government after winning general elections in 1991, but surrendered power after 11 months in office after failing to win backing for radical reforms.
A total of 31 parties and coalitions will contest the poll on April 19, but only four or five have any chance of winning seats in the assembly.
